segments.text: Chapter 8 — Legitimacy Over Time
The Handoff After the Surge
A regional hospital network is six months past a capacity surge.
The outgoing administrator had emergency authority to override local staffing rules, fast-track purchasing, and require central sign-off on decisions that used to stay local.
At the handoff meeting, the incoming administrator inherits the same authority package.
Nobody argues for crisis powers as a new policy.
They are simply listed as current operating permissions.
In week two, a local site asks to resume its old staffing rotation for one unit.
The center declines and keeps surge-era central control in place "until further review." The review date is left open.
No one says the decision is wrong.
No one says who can reopen it.
Leadership transfer is where legitimacy becomes easiest to read.
People can see who is followed, why they are followed, and what it now costs to question direction.
Start from the handoff, not from an abstract definition.
The hospital scene is not an exception case.
It shows the structure in plain view.
Here is how to read that structure at transfer: after authority passes, people keep following for different reasons.
Those reasons are different forms of legitimacy, and each one ties authority to accountability in a different way.
Why People Continue to Follow
Legitimacy changes over time.
It can renew, transfer, harden, or drift out of step with what is actually happening.
Across transfers, the reasons differ.
In one, people follow because they can still watch conduct and test it against consequence.
In another, they follow because procedure assigned the role.
In another, because the title already carries permission.
In another, because questioning the transfer starts to sound like betrayal.
The same institution can move through all four over time.
The question is not who has good motives.
The question is what keeps authority revisable once it changes hands.
Example-Based Legitimacy
In example-based legitimacy, people keep following when they can see the new
leader's behavior line up with what leadership asks of everyone else.
Stay with the hospital network.
The incoming administrator publicly narrows one inherited emergency override after local teams show stable performance and clear safety outcomes.
She accepts a slower rollout, keeps the exception list visible, and names the conditions for reopening central control if risk rises.
People are not following only because she has the role.
They follow because they can see conduct tied to consequence in real time.
That pattern lasts only if what leaders do keeps matching what they say—especially
under pressure.
Procedural Legitimacy
In procedural legitimacy, people keep following when transfer rules still limit
what leaders can do.
Stay in the same network.
The board's transfer protocol requires a published review of all surge-era permissions within ninety days, local testimony from affected sites, and a recorded vote for each exception that remains.
The incoming administrator keeps authority because the process says she has it, but the process also limits what can pass forward without scrutiny.
When the process is real, work keeps moving and challenge keeps a door open.
When procedure becomes ceremony, continuity can hide erosion.
Office-Based Legitimacy
In office-based legitimacy, people follow because the position already carries
permissions that transfer with the title.
Stay in the same network.

The incoming administrator keeps broad central sign-off authority because "that is what this office now includes." Local leaders route decisions through the center by default even when the original surge condition is gone.
Nothing dramatic happens on the surface.
The path simply stays centralized because the role already carries it.
This form can stabilize large systems.
It can also move authority forward faster than accountability can catch up.
Sacralized Legitimacy
Sacralized legitimacy appears when questioning the transfer starts to feel like a moral or identity threat.
People follow because challenge to leadership starts to sound like challenge to who "we" are.
Stay in the same network.
A clinical director asks whether surge-era controls should sunset unit by unit.
The reply is not about metrics or process.
It is that reopening transfer decisions now would "undermine trust in the mission we held together during crisis." After that exchange, fewer people raise transfer questions in public.
From the inside, this can feel like unity.
Structurally, it makes correction harder: challenge becomes socially costly, then rare.
How Legitimacy Transfers and Shifts
Under pressure, many groups slide along a familiar arc—from example-based
legitimacy, toward procedural legitimacy, then office-based legitimacy, then
sacralized legitimacy.
In plain language, people trust what they can see, then what the rules assign,
then what the title already carries, and sometimes the role grows too charged to
question openly.
That drift is common; it is not inevitable.
Groups in renewal deliberately reopen transfer decisions before insulation hardens.
Crisis matters because it can widen office permissions quickly.
Without active rollback, those permissions are what the next leader inherits.
Selective Followership as a Probe
Selective followership works as a probe: it hints which form of legitimacy is
active and what kind of correction still has room.
Not all refusal means disorder.
In vibrant groups, selective refusal can function as correction.
People can say, "I agree with the goal, but not this method," without becoming enemies of the group.
That limited pushback protects judgment and keeps authority connected to consequences.
In decaying groups, selective refusal turns covert.
People perform agreement while quietly routing around decisions they do not trust.
The group still looks coordinated, but shared reality weakens.
The same outward behavior can track renewal or erosion.
Open selective dissent usually points toward renewal.
Hidden selective resistance usually points toward erosion.
Open disagreement inside shared purpose usually means legitimacy is still renewing.
Public compliance paired with private divergence usually means legitimacy is sliding toward office-based or sacralized forms.
In that state, calm surfaces can hide trust loss, and open challenge can give way to Disagreement is Suppressed.
Legitimacy and Accountability
A leader can still draw attention after legitimacy weakens.
What lingers are the titles, the stories about who we are, and the habits that keep repeating.
The structural question is whether people making decisions remain accountable to
the people their choices affect.
If legitimacy cannot renew through visible correction, influence may continue,
but decay deepens.
Correction and Circulation
People keep following for different legitimacy reasons.

The earlier distinction still applies here: correction asks whether warnings can still change what formal leaders decide; circulation asks whether anyone else may hold the decision point for a stretch and return without a penalty round.
How those episodes are treated feeds legitimacy as well as throughput.
Permission—what the room teaches after someone leads without being the usual name—adds up in the same vibrant or decaying habits circulation describes.
Before long, who counts as a leader and who people will still follow stop looking like separate questions.
Watch the ordinary traces.
For correction: whether bad news travels without career penalty, and whether dissent can change a decision before execution.
For circulation: whether step-ins are credited and named, whether people are welcome back into the decision ring, and whether the afterward story reads as useful work or damage control.
When correction signals read closed, authority is becoming one-way.
When permission reads cold, people learn to wait for the usual gate even when the work has already moved on.
What gets rewarded or punished while those paths narrow is what the next leaders will copy—**Leadership Reproduces Itself**.
Scale and Distance
Under scale, distance and abstraction make correction harder to sustain.
A short-lived tight grip on correction during crisis can harden into habit if nobody deliberately opens feedback again.
As reach grows, decision-makers often sit farther from consequence, and structure
slides toward insulation.
Correction is not a promise.
It helps groups adjust as they grow—but only when feedback can still change decisions.
Return to the hospital handoff.
The unresolved question was never whether central control existed; it was who could reopen it and on what terms.
By now that read is clearer.
Example-based, procedural, office-based, and sacralized pressures each answer that reopening question differently.
That difference decides whether transfer keeps accountability alive—or seals it.
Appendix A extends this transfer read across government, healthcare, and religious
institutional sequences at larger scale.
Legitimacy survives through repeated accountability, not one-time assent.
